I found Cho Seon-ok after a long time.

This place has been loved by people of all ages for a long time and is famous for its seasoned beef ribs.

Actually, I can't eat there all the time because of the price, but it's one of the few restaurants that leaves me impressed every time I go.
Personally, I really like radish soup ordered with seasoned beef ribs, but the price has gone up before I know it.

Side dishes are served as soon as you order, and since the meat is grilled directly over a charcoal fire, it takes a bit of time, but the waiting time is enjoyable.

Finally, we received seasoned beef ribs!
Perhaps because it is marinated in seasoning and then grilled over a charcoal fire, the unique flavor makes it difficult to put down your chopsticks.
it's good!
It seems like everything can be expressed in this one word.

The galbitang served on the side was also made by boiling beef bone broth and meat broth separately, so it was full of meat in a white broth and featured thick glass noodles.

If you eat the style of rib soup that your mother used to make with rice, you will feel full all day long and will not feel hungry.

This place is also famous for its naengmyeon (naengmyeon), which is Pyongyang style naengmyeon and has a smooth taste.

Looking forward to your next visit...

reviews.author: taeho Kim
reviews.text:
-
Atmosphere:

I feel like I'm in a shabby, rough country restaurant. I went there on a Sunday, and there were a steady stream of customers coming after hiking. People of all ages come here mainly, and it is a restaurant that is reasonably priced and easy to stop by.
However, rather than being clean, there seems to be a slightly musty smell inside or around the store, so I recommend going with friends of the same sex.

-
Flavor:

It is said that it was the first restaurant in Seoul to sell makguksu and the first to feature tray makguksu on its menu. Is that right?
Anyway, out of curiosity, I tried to order Makguksu seasoned and Chogye seasoned together, but they did not recommend it because the difference was whether buckwheat noodles or chicken meat were added to the same seasoning. So, I ordered regular makguksu (₩6,000) + seasoned chogye (₩14,000) + steamed dumplings (₩7,000).

Makguksu (₩6,000) is served in a bibim noodle style with chicken toppings, and can be eaten water noodle style by adding broth later. The taste of the makguksu was slightly sweet and the sesame oil taste was a bit strong. There was no special edge to the seasoning, so it tasted more ordinary than I expected. However, when I ate Makguksu with chicken toppings, the combination of textures and flavors made it taste very attractive. After pouring in the broth, does it taste like slurping? It was nice to eat more comfortably.

The chogye seasoned salad (₩14,000) had chicken seasoned with lettuce and vegetables, and it was a visual that stimulated the salivary glands. The seasoning seems to be the same as Makguksu, but the seasoning and vegetables mixed with the soft meat make it more delicious than noodles. The portions are generous, so it seems like a good dish for multiple people to order.

The steamed dumplings (₩7,000) looked delicious, plump and shiny. The beef is made from pork and vegetables and uses a certain thickness of blood, which is familiar but comfortably delicious. If you dip steamed dumplings in soy sauce or vinegar seasoning, they will become slightly spicy and you will be able to enjoy an even better taste.

Lastly, I added buckwheat pancakes (₩7,000), which were ordinary but delicious. I was so full that I left it, but it was slightly thick and had just the right amount of vegetables, so it had a comforting taste.

*
Overall, although the price is not expensive, I think it is a place where you can have a good value for money meal because the portions are generous. However, in terms of hygiene, it feels a bit musty, so I recommend going only with friends you are comfortable with. I heard that steamed chicken and chicken gomtang are also popular. I haven't tried them, but I can imagine what they'll be like when I try the other menu items.

I didn't know what would happen, so I just left and went to a restaurant that brought back memories rather than wasting money.

reviews.author: Bart Chang
reviews.text:
It could be said to be the standard of a field camp.
Now is the perfect season to go.
Although the temperature is over 30 degrees during the day, a cool breeze draws me here as the sun sets.
As I enter the narrow alley, the fragrant smell of pork belly is astounding. I was assigned a seat and ordered pork belly. It's a strange store where you can bring your own alcohol and leave the fish to the cat.
After putting the meat on the grill, spreading the mushrooms, kimchi and leaf mustard kimchi, we share a glass of cold beer to quench our thirst. All the worries in the world are gone now that the beer that sells in an instant makes all my worries disappear.

Sweet pork belly, savory grilled kimchi, and crunchy red lettuce are eaten like samhap. This is the triad of Daewonjip.

There is no need to worry about the fried rice because it is made with a master craftsman.
My father-in-law, who had been frying everything on bare rice for years, did it so amazingly that a bottle of soju and a bottle of beer flew into the air toward Eulji.

This house is a treasure.

Because the table is the size of the table outside the convenience store.

reviews.text:
A low-temperature cooked tonkatsu restaurant in Euljiro. There seems to be a wait usually, but luckily I didn't have to wait and went right in. There is bar seating and two tables for two.

♤ Assorted Katsu (22,000₩)
♤ Mini Curry (4,500₩)

Assorted katsu consists of sirloin, tenderloin, and chicken tenderloin katsu. Katsura's batter, made by maturing Jeju black pork at a low temperature for two weeks and then frying it at a low temperature, is soft and oily. The meat also has a soft texture, possibly due to aging. It's clear that they put a lot of effort into the tonkatsu, but personally, I thought it was a bit greasy. I think it's because it's cooked at a low temperature, so it's oily and gets soggy quickly. There seems to be quite a difference in likes and dislikes. Not recommended for those who like crispy fries. Still, I liked the texture and flavor of the meat itself.

The curry contains a lot of onions and has a sweet taste like onion soup. They instruct you to mix the chives and bread crumbs before eating.

Due to the cooking method, it takes about 15 to 20 minutes for the food to come out after ordering, so take this into account.

It has a very soft texture and the batter has no presence, to the point where you wonder if it is soggy. Perhaps because this is a place that avoids sauces, they only serve salt and commercially available sauces, but as I ate it, it was so greasy that I couldn't help but want to eat a bowl of Yukgaejang cup ramen. I also ordered a mini curry, but it tasted like a commercial curry rather than a handmade one... I thought this was a place that really focused on pork cutlet. This place has completely different reviews depending on your taste, so although it is a bit expensive, I recommend trying it once.

From unusual signboards to long-established makhoe restaurants that invite excessive drinking, and night market stalls, it is a great place to enjoy a drink while enjoying the atmosphere. It's okay as a daytime drink or a second or third place, but it's probably hard to come out sober.

On a quiet Saturday lunch, I stopped by to replenish my lack of alcohol and simply ordered a plate of raw fish. The main menu is makhoe, but other dishes include gwamegi, boiled octopus, raw raw fish, and raw fish rice bowl.

The basic side dish is a simple set of stir-fried anchovies and bean sprout soup, which are very useful as a side dish with drinks. There was no end to the sweet and salty stir-fried anchovies, and the bean sprout soup was very refreshing.

Makhoe is a seasoned sashimi dish made with freshly caught fish by sailors, but the types of fish used are not always consistent. The last meal I received that day included flounder and herring.

Various vegetables such as cucumbers, onions, crown crowns, and water parsley were placed on the side of the flounder and herring, and sesame seeds were sprinkled on top. Now add our unique seasoning and mix well and you are ready to eat.

The owner added the seasoning himself and mixed it with a brilliant hand, so the ratio to the raw fish was just right. The base is sour and spicy red pepper paste, but it's not at all harsh and clean, so it's a drug.

To be honest, it was difficult to feel the original taste of the raw fish because it was covered by the seasoning, but the savory flavor came out as I chewed it with a small knife. I tried wrapping it with seaweed and it went very well.

The combination of savory seaweed and seasoning sauce is versatile, and since the sekkosi has a texture, I felt like the seaweed was covering it well. If I hadn't been full, I would have mixed the rice and wrapped it in seaweed, but it was a bit disappointing.

reviews.author: ch. “Connoisseur” Paik
reviews.text:
John Ramen (4.1/5.0)
Tonkotsu Ramen ₩10,000 / Additional Char Siu ₩3,000 / Chicken Karaage (2 pieces) ₩3,000

In Chungmuro Printing Alley, where tribes and forklifts are everywhere, a quiet race begins every day with one destination in mind. When you see the 'ㅈ' sign, it's the finish line. Only those in 9th place can take a seat, and those in 10th place have to wait about 20 minutes more. This is a John Ramen open run race. Since it is a small establishment with only 9 seats, I am concerned about the dining environment, but the spacing between all counter seats is not too uncomfortable. The female staff's response is deeply ingrained with kindness.

I sit down lightly on a high chair and read the ‘Usage Guide’ carefully. I like the music that fills the store, so I find it and add it to my playlist. PREP's 'On and On'. Meanwhile, the ramen is arriving one after another in order of waiting. Inside the round white pottery, there are two pieces of uncut pork belly pork wrapped all around. One sheet is included as standard and one additional sheet is included. The whisk, round sliced ​​green onions, menma, and intact ajidama further heighten the anticipation of the taste.

When I took a bite of the soup, my first impression was that it wasn't very special, but the more I ate it, the more it became quite thick. It's not heavy, but the body that lingers in your mouth is close to being a little dry. Even though Kyokai broth is added, the sea flavor is not strong. And the most notable feature is that, perhaps due to the small amount of tare, the salt content is very low, so even diners who are averse to the strong saltiness of Japanese ramen will definitely enjoy it.

The noodles are thin and cooked to a chewy texture. In the middle, I came across the ends of five or six noodle strands that were clumped together, and I felt a little bit shaken while slurping down the noodle strands. Menma is sweet and soft, with a moderate crunchiness remaining at the end.

The char siu is thick and long, just like a serving of pork ordered at an old pork belly restaurant, giving visual satisfaction. If you look closely, the way you eat is the key, so you have to find a way that is comfortable for you and eat it yourself. Unlike the fat part that can be cut with a spoon, a very small part of the meat can only be cut with the mouth, which makes me feel a little cold sweat. Five or six mouth scissors are required. The moderate salty sweetness coexists with the savory flavor, and the scent of torch fire and soft ginger permeates.

I put off the karaage that came with a warning to be careful because it was hot, but now I'm paying attention. Even on the outside, it looks like it's moist. When eaten together with mayo sauce and pickled onions, which have a bit of a spicy kick from the addition of chopped peppers, the juicy and sweet-salty mix creates an amazing taste.

Returning to the ramen, I cut the ajidama I had saved in half and it was perfectly half-boiled. There is a slight sweetness, but it lacks the feeling of being combined with the broth, making it mysterious.  Ask for a bowl of cucumber mesh to end the meal. Thanks to the low salt content, there is no burden when rolling it up and eating it.

This is John Ramen, where the time invested in the open run race is not a waste, and it is not at all awkward to honestly express '#I'm delicious'.

reviews.author: B K
reviews.text:
A Chinese restaurant that is close to perfection in terms of taste.
It's hard to find a decent Chinese restaurant these days, but this restaurant meets the taste we expect from a good old Chinese restaurant.
Ganjajang is a proper soybean paste that is easy to eat and has a lot of contents. The fried meat is the best to eat because the batter is crispy enough but not too thick.
It's hard to find a place that sells Nanjawanse these days, but you can find it here. It's lightly fried on the outside and then cooked in starch-based seasoning. When the fried food on the outside and the thick seasoning come together, it feels a bit like scorched rice.
It's a delicious restaurant in many ways, but since the spacing between tables is narrow and it's an old store, the neat feel is limited, so take that into account.

reviews.text:
It's a pretty famous kalguksu restaurant, and it's been almost 5 years since I've been there.
This house is still doing well in business.
There was a wait, but I quickly left so I could get in.
I ordered kal mandu soup and kimchi fried rice with the intention of sharing it with my group. Kalmandu soup is topped with seasoned minced meat, which enriches the otherwise boring taste. There are two dumplings and they are quite large so they are easy to eat.
Overall, it's a delicious dumpling soup, but in fact, I think the kek of this restaurant is game chi fried rice. It's very irritating, but the stimulation is just right for eating, so it goes on and on.
It's fried rice with a lot of oil, but it has a strong savory taste, and in many ways, it's a taste you'll want to try at home if you know the recipe.
